idiom_name: JUnit Jupiter @Test/@BeforeEach in a Kotlin class with lateinit fields
implementation_notes: JUnit Jupiter annotations work unchanged from Kotlin: @BeforeEach initialises lateinit fields for the arrange beat, the @Test body performs one act, and the assert beat uses kotlin.test helpers (assertEquals/assertTrue) or JUnit's Assertions as a qualified call. The classic fixture class is the test class itself, which fits Kotlin because data classes and default arguments shrink most arrange boilerplate, and @DisplayName carries the given/when/then phrasing into the report.
pitfalls: lateinit gives no early failure: a test that skips the shared setup throws UninitializedPropertyAccessException at the act beat, which reads like a production bug rather than a broken arrange.
Kotlin's default visibility is public, but a private test class or method is not run by JUnit and discovery reports 'no tests found' instead of an error.
assertEquals(expected, actual) takes the expected value first; swapping the operands still passes and inverts the failure report.

variants.name: Kotest BehaviorSpec with given/when/then blocks
variants.implementation_notes: Kotest makes the Given-When-Then vocabulary first-class block functions: BehaviorSpec provides context/given/when/then (plus title-case variants because when is a Kotlin keyword, hence the backticks), the given block carries the arrange beat, the when block the act, and each then block an assertion. State shared by sibling then blocks stays in the enclosing scope, lifecycle hooks (BeforeTest/BeforeSpec) cover cross-test fixtures, and the classic class-per-fixture structure is replaced by nested DSL scopes.
pitfalls: Spec bodies execute during discovery: constructing expensive fixtures in the class body or in an outer given repeats them for every leaf test path, so build per-test state in the innermost scope or in hooks.
Because when is a Kotlin keyword, forgetting the backticks or the When title-case variant produces a confusing compile error inside the DSL rather than a test failure.
Kotest matchers (shouldBe) and kotlin.test assertions can be mixed, but their failure output differs; stay with one vocabulary so the assert beat reports consistently.
